commenti.body:
I felt the same way on my first watch, but having seen it a few more times, it lands a lot better with me now. The tonal shift is abrupt but intentional.  

What else is there to really see in those final moments besides wallowing in Moonie's misery? We know CPS will find and take her away soon. There's no saving her. Nothing for the audience to chew beyond a child's pain, I'd prefer the escapism.

Sean Baker could have had it play out straightforwardly and given us a really bleak and sad ending. But imo the actual ending is just as devastating and depressing, but it's a little more creative and satisfying to the themes of the film.

I hated it so much. It's like, "Don't feel bad at all, it's all gonna work out." It's an easy escape, even if you believe it's a fantasy or ambiguous or whatever, the film is still objectively trying to leave you with a happy emotion. And it's so lazy in how it executes it; for a movie mostly shot on film, that even printed the digital parts to film so it'd all look like film, to just hard cut to an iPhone is goofy as hell and loses all respect from me as an audience member. It's like pouring hot garbage into your eyes and emotions to prove that it's different and exciting, when before it was one of the best modern films I'd seen in a long time.
I 100% agree and this is what I thought when I first watched it

It emphasizes their miserable life right next to the fake puffy factory of happiness. All of child's dreams are there, and when the reality becomes absolutely unbearable, she goes there in her imagination. I think it's obvious that it's not happening in reality - I saw it ages ago, but I think even the saturation and brightness are changing in the epilogue. I saw it as similar to Del Toro's Pan's Labyrinth, where the girl goes into her imaginary world when the reality is becoming unbearable.
I found it to be poignant
It’s obviously not trying for a happy ending lol, Moonie’s life is left in complete shambles and we end on her doing something desperately sad.

I loved this film and I loved the ending! The girls' fate is inescapable; short of a miracle, their prospects in life dire. I took this desperate, frenetic flight that ends the film as a kind of gift from the film maker, like something he was giving the characters in his story because he knows, and the audience knows, that in real life they have nothing. Whether the events depicted in this sequence are 'real' or not (because it is conceivable they are real) doesn't matter. The change in the quality of the film tells us we're stepping out of the story - the film is leaving the story behind because it has no ending. Generational trauma - poverty - neglect - it's a cycle from which there is rarely an out. This is what the ending is - it's an out, and the fact that we low-key know it's not 'real' gives it, for me, a genuine sense of tragedy. 

Personally I'm a fan of endings like this, where film makers abandon their narratives in the last moments. It was a favourite device of Kiarostami, most obviously in the ending of Taste Of Cherry where the film switches to hand-held video and we see footage that looks like it's taken from a 'behind the scenes' extra feature. 

I haven't seen it for a long time, but I have a vague memory that The 400 Blows does something a bit similar at the end (?).

I know what you’re saying and agree to some extent. At that point in the film I was on the verge of a cathartic emotional reaction and ready to sit with it.

But I think as others have noted that the escapism is a really powerful choice as well, especially as it’s the child characters’ inner reaction to the situation not my own adult detached viewer reaction.

The other thing that makes it a really impactful ending (if perhaps somewhat overly-intellectualized) is the way it finally grapples with the looming spectre of Disney/Capitalism/a society that excludes and marginalizes people like the main characters of the film while simultaneously being at the center of their reality. The real life context that Disney doesn’t allow filming in the park adds to this shocking jolt of socio-economic fantasy in a way that is both surprising and brings us back to the meta-awareness of the experience of watching a movie.
The ending of The Holy Mountain also comes to mind in this list.

Yes, The 400 Blows has an ending which I assume was a reference point for Baker, with the boy sprinting away from his confinement in a  school in a great tracking shot before ending at the sea, where he has nowhere else to run. It's actually bleaker than The Florida Project because Truffaut pulls the reality that this child's prospects are very bleak back to the foreground at the last minute, rather than letting you sit in a bittersweet fantasy as Baker does.

I didn't interpret it as imaginary at all, I thought they actually did sneak into Disneyworld and run through it as a last ditch attempt to "escape" the situation. Granted, this wasn't going to have the desired outcome, as they would inevitably get busted and kicked out, but I think maybe that was also sort of the point being driven home; that we can still find happiness, even if it's fleeting happiness when we know there's really no escape from a tragic ending, through friendship.
